Reprobation (Doctrine)
rep-ruh-BAY-shun
noun (Reformed soteriology)
From Latin reprobare (to reject, disapprove). The doctrine, the dark side of the decree of predestination, that God, in His sovereign justice, has from eternity passed by the non-elect (preterition) and ordained them to dishonor and wrath for their sin, for the glory of His justice. Westminster Confession III; Romans 9:21-22.

📖 Biblical Definition

From Latin reprobare (to reject, disapprove); the doctrine, the dark and solemn side of the decree of predestination, that God in His sovereign justice has from eternity decreed concerning the non-elect. The Westminster Confession (III.3, 7) holds that, by the decree of God, for the manifestation of His glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life, and others foreordained to everlasting death; concerning the non-elect (III.7): The rest of mankind, God was pleased, according to the unsearchable counsel of his own will, whereby he extendeth or withholdeth mercy as he pleaseth, for the glory of his sovereign power over his creatures, to pass by, and to ordain them to dishonour and wrath for their sin, to the praise of his glorious justice. The doctrine of reprobation has two aspects, carefully distinguished: (1) preterition (the passing by) — God's sovereign decree to pass by the non-elect, not choosing them to salvation, withholding the saving grace He freely bestows on the elect; this is an act of God's sovereign will (He extends or withholds mercy as He pleases, Romans 9:18); (2) condemnation (the ordaining to wrath) — God's decree to ordain the non-elect to dishonor and wrath FOR THEIR SIN; the ground of the condemnation is the sinner's own sin (the reprobate are justly condemned for their own sin, not arbitrarily), while the ground of election is God's sovereign grace alone. The crucial asymmetry: election is unconditional (God chooses the elect not on the basis of any good in them but according to His sovereign grace), but reprobation's condemnation is conditioned on the sinner's own sin (God ordains the reprobate to wrath for their sin, justly); God is not the author of the sinner's sin (the sinner sins freely and is justly responsible), but God's sovereign decree to pass by the non-elect and to condemn them justly for their sin is part of His eternal counsel. The biblical foundation: Romans 9:18-23 (God has mercy on whom He will, and whom He will He hardens; the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction); Proverbs 16:4 (the LORD has made all things for Himself, yea, even the wicked for the day of evil); 1 Peter 2:8 (those who stumble at the word, being disobedient, whereunto also they were appointed); Jude 1:4 (certain men ordained to this condemnation). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of reprobation with appropriate solemnity and care: it is the dark side of the decree of predestination; it involves preterition (God's sovereign passing by) and just condemnation (for the sinner's own sin); it is grounded in God's sovereign justice and serves the manifestation of His glory; God is not the author of sin, and the reprobate are justly condemned for their own sin; the doctrine is to be handled with reverence, not speculation, and held alongside the free offer of the gospel to all and the genuine responsibility of all who hear.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

From Latin reprobare (to reject); the dark side of predestination: God's eternal decree to pass by the non-elect (preterition) and ordain them to dishonor and wrath for their sin (condemnation), for the glory of His justice (Westminster III.7; Romans 9:18-23); election unconditional, but reprobation's condemnation conditioned on the sinner's own sin.

REPROBATION (DOCTRINE), n. (Reformed soteriology; Latin reprobare, to reject) The dark side of the decree of predestination: God's eternal decree concerning the non-elect. Westminster III.7: God was pleased, according to the unsearchable counsel of His will, to pass by the rest of mankind, and to ordain them to dishonour and wrath for their sin, to the praise of His glorious justice. Two aspects: (1) preterition (the passing by — God's sovereign decree not to choose them to salvation, withholding saving grace, Romans 9:18); (2) condemnation (ordaining to wrath FOR THEIR SIN — the ground of condemnation is the sinner's own sin). The asymmetry: election unconditional (sovereign grace), reprobation's condemnation conditioned on the sinner's sin (just). God not the author of sin. Foundation: Romans 9:18-23; Proverbs 16:4; 1 Peter 2:8; Jude 1:4.

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 9:18 — "Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth."

Romans 9:22 — "What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction?"

Proverbs 16:4 — "The LORD hath made all things for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil."

1 Peter 2:8 — "And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Reprobation is the dark side of predestination, involving preterition (God's sovereign passing by) and just condemnation (for the sinner's own sin); the corruptions are the denial of reprobation (a one-sided predestinarianism) and the hyper-Calvinist or fatalist distortion that makes God the author of sin or denies the sinner's responsibility.

expand to see more

The doctrine of reprobation must be handled with appropriate solemnity and care, held against several distortions. The denial of reprobation (a one-sided predestinarianism that affirms election but denies any decree concerning the non-elect) fails to account for the biblical witness to God's sovereign dealing with the non-elect (Romans 9:18, 22; Proverbs 16:4; 1 Peter 2:8; Jude 1:4) and for the logical entailment of unconditional election (if God sovereignly chooses some to salvation, He thereby passes by the rest). The hyper-Calvinist or fatalist distortion makes God the author of the sinner's sin, or denies the genuine responsibility of the reprobate, or treats reprobation as an arbitrary condemnation apart from the sinner's sin; this contradicts the biblical doctrine that God is not the author of sin (James 1:13), that the reprobate are justly condemned for their own sin, and that all who hear the gospel are genuinely responsible to respond. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine with reverence and care, observing the crucial asymmetry between election and reprobation: election is unconditional (God chooses the elect not on the basis of any good foreseen in them, but according to His sovereign grace alone); but reprobation's condemnation is conditioned on the sinner's own sin (God ordains the reprobate to wrath FOR THEIR SIN, justly — the ground of condemnation is the sinner's sin, not an arbitrary divine decree apart from sin). Reprobation involves two aspects: preterition (the sovereign passing by, an act of God's will) and just condemnation (for the sinner's own sin). God is not the author of sin; the reprobate sin freely and are justly responsible and justly condemned. The doctrine serves the manifestation of God's glory (the glory of His justice in the just condemnation of sin, as election serves the glory of His grace in the salvation of sinners). The patriarchal-Reformed reader handles the doctrine with reverence, not speculation; holds it alongside the free and genuine offer of the gospel to all (the gospel is to be freely offered to all, and all who hear are genuinely responsible to respond); and rests in the sovereign justice and wisdom of God, whose judgments are unsearchable and whose ways are past finding out (Romans 11:33).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin reprobare; the dark side of predestination; preterition (sovereign passing by) and just condemnation (for the sinner's sin); the asymmetry with unconditional election; Westminster III.7; Romans 9:18-23; God not the author of sin.
